'''Challenge–dechallenge–rechallenge''' ('''CDR''') is a medical testing [[Protocol (natural sciences)|protocol]] in which a medicine or drug is administered, withdrawn, then re-administered, while being monitored for [[Adverse effect (medicine)|adverse effects]] at each stage.  The protocol is used when [[Statistics|statistical testing]] is inappropriate due to an idiosyncratic reaction by a specific individual, or a lack of sufficient test subjects and unit of analysis is the individual.  During the dechallenge (withdrawal) phase, the medication is allowed to wash out of the system in order to determine what effect the medication is having on an individual.

==Use in drug testing==
CDR is one means of establishing the validity and benefits of medication in treating specific conditions<ref name="pmid3821430">{{cite journal |author=Spitzer WO |title=Importance of valid measurements of benefit and risk |journal=Med Toxicol |volume=1 |pages=74–8 |year=1986 |issue=Suppl 1 |pmid=3821430 }}</ref> as well as any [[adverse drug reaction]]s.  The [[Food and Drug Administration]] of the United States lists positive dechallenge reactions (an adverse event which disappears on withdrawal of the medication) as well as negative (an adverse event which continues after withdrawal), as well as positive rechallenge (symptoms re-occurring on re-administration) and negative rechallenge (failure of a symptom to re-occur after re-administration).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fda.gov/medwatch/report/cberguid/define.htm |title=Guideline for Adverse Experience Reporting for Licensed Biological Products: Definitions |publisher=[[Food and Drug Administration]] |access-date=2008-03-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071007215452/https://www.fda.gov/medwatch/report/cberguid/define.htm |archive-date=2007-10-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  It is one of the standard means of assessing adverse drug reactions in France.<ref name="pmid10268556">{{cite journal |author=Begaud B |title=Standardized assessment of adverse drug reactions: the method used in France. Special workshop—clinical |journal=Drug Inf J |volume=18 |issue=3–4 |pages=275–81 |year=1984 |pmid=10268556 |doi=10.1177/009286158401800314|s2cid=42797865 }}</ref>

==Fluoxetine and suicide==
{{main|Fluoxetine}}
[[Peter Breggin]] asserted that there was an association between [[fluoxetine]] (Prozac) use and [[suicidal ideation|suicidal thoughts]]. While his research group were investigating the effectiveness and side effects of the medication, Breggin noticed that only certain individuals responded to the medication with increased thoughts of suicide, and used the challenge–dechallenge–rechallenge protocol in an effort to verify the link. Given the low occurrence rate of suicidality, statistical testing was considered inappropriate.<ref>{{cite book |author=Breggin, Ginger Ross |author2=Breggin, Peter Roger |title=Talking back to Prozac: what doctors won't tell you about today's most controversial drug |publisher=St. Martin's Paperbacks |location=New York |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-312-95606-6 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/talkingbacktopro00pete }}</ref>  Other researchers have similarly suggested that the CDR is useful for researching the [[Adverse drug reaction|adverse effect]] of suicidality while taking fluoxetine, and [[Eli Lilly and Company|Eli Lilly]] adopted the protocol rather than [[randomized controlled trial]]s when testing for increased risk of suicide.<ref name=Maris>{{cite web|last=Maris |first=RWM |title=Suicide and Neuropsychiatric Adverse Effects of SSRI Medications: Methodological Issues |date=2002-10-04 |location=[[Philadelphia]], Pennsylvania |access-date=2008-03-15 |url=http://www.oism.info/en/therapy/theory/suicide_and_neuropsychiatric_adverse_effects_of_ssri.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081120204712/http://www.oism.info/en/therapy/theory/suicide_and_neuropsychiatric_adverse_effects_of_ssri.htm |archive-date=November 20, 2008 }}</ref> In addition to suicidality, [[akathisia]] is a reaction to medication which is suggested as amenable to a CDR protocol.<ref name="pmid14517576">{{cite journal |vauthors=Healy D, Whitaker C |title=Antidepressants and suicide: risk-benefit conundrums |journal=J Psychiatry Neurosci |volume=28 |issue=5 |pages=331–7 |year=2003 |pmid=14517576 |pmc=193979}}</ref><ref name="pmid12601224">{{cite journal |author=Healy D |title=Lines of evidence on the risks of suicide with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors |journal=Psychother Psychosom |volume=72 |issue=2 |pages=71–9 |year=2003 |pmid=12601224 |doi=10.1159/000068691|s2cid=1583644 }}</ref>

[[Clinical trial]]s using a CDR protocol are also reported for clinicians attempting to assess the effects of a medication on patients.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Rothschild AJ, Locke CA |title=Reexposure to fluoxetine after serious suicide attempts by three patients: the role of akathisia |journal=J Clin Psychiatry |volume=52 |issue=12 |pages=491–3 |year=1991 |pmid=1752848 }}
</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Banu AB, Alias Balamurugan SA, Thirumalaikolundusubramanian P |title=Detection of dechallenge in spontaneous reporting systems: A comparison of Bayes methods |journal=Indian J Pharmacol |volume=46 |issue=3|pages=277–80 |year=2014|doi=10.4103/0253-7613.132157|pmid=24987173 |pmc=4071703 |doi-access=free }}
</ref>
